domains.title: Moon God of the Night
domains.subtitle: Lunar Order, Separation, and Celestial Sibling
domains.lead: Tsukuyomi is the moon kami of Japanese myth, born from Izanagi's right eye during the purification that also produced Amaterasu from the left eye and Susanoo from the nose. He governs the night and the lunar calendar, and his mythology turns on a violent act that separated him forever from the sun.

mythology.lead: Tsukuyomi's mythology is shorter than that of his siblings but crucial for understanding the separation of sun and moon.

myths.title: Birth from Izanagi's Eye
myths.text: After escaping Yomi, Izanagi purified himself in a river. As he washed his right eye, Tsukuyomi was born. Amaterasu was given rule over the day, Tsukuyomi over the night, and Susanoo over the sea. The three siblings divided the cosmos among themselves.

myths.title: The Killing of Uke-mochi
myths.text: Amaterasu sent Tsukuyomi to visit Uke-mochi, the goddess of food. Uke-mochi produced food by vomiting or defecating it from her body. Disgusted or offended by this, Tsukuyomi killed her. Amaterasu was so angry that she declared she would never look at him again, and the sun and moon were separated into day and night.

myths.title: Sun and Moon Divided
myths.text: The myth explains why the sun and moon do not appear together. Tsukuyomi's act of violence created the alternation of day and night and established the moon as a separate, nocturnal power.

lore.syncretism: Tsukuyomi is less prominent in Japanese religion than Amaterasu or Susanoo, but he appears in calendars, poetry, and astral symbolism. His separation from the sun reflects a common Eurasian motif of the divided celestial siblings, while his specific myth is shaped by Japanese ideas of purity and pollution.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tsukuyomi appears in Japanese literature, anime, and games as a cool, nocturnal counterpart to the solar Amaterasu. The moon remains a major theme in Japanese poetry and art, and Tsukuyomi's name is invoked in works that explore the night and its mysteries.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tsukuyomi is the night that follows the day. His separation from Amaterasu reminds us that even divine siblings can wound each other beyond repair, and that some divisions — like sun and moon — become the structure of the world.
lore.archaeology: Tsukuyomi has few independent shrines. His significance is preserved in textual mythology and in the astronomical and calendrical traditions that divide the sun's domain from the moon's.
